slides.title: Pillars of Personal Finance
slides.kicker: Paanch pillars, one strong money life!
bullets: Personal finance stands on five pillars: income, budgeting, saving, investing, and protection and risk management.
Income is the money you receive, such as a salary or business income, and it is the starting point of everything.
Budgeting decides how much to save, how much to spend, and how one spends that money on needs and wants.
Protection means safeguarding your money and assets through insurance and debt management.
slides.note: Ek bimaar pillar, poori table hilti hai — keep all five strong.

slides.title: Income Comes First
slides.kicker: No income, no spending, saving or investing.
bullets: Income is money a person receives regularly or occasionally in return for products sold or services rendered.
A teacher earns a monthly salary, a shopkeeper earns business profits, and a person earns rent from letting out property.
An investor earns interest from bank deposits, while a shareholder receives dividends and interest from securities.
Earn While You Learn programmes let college students earn through part-time work, internships or apprenticeships while gaining real-world skills.
slides.note: Think: which skill of yours could earn money one day?

slides.title: Budget: A Written Plan
slides.kicker: Write it down, watch impulse spending go.
bullets: Budgeting means planning in advance how income will be spent; a budget is a written plan that aims to balance income and expenses.
A family may plan monthly spending on food, rent, school fees and transport, and decide how much to save each month.
Financial goals like a school trip next month, sports equipment after six months, higher education, or emergencies help prioritise needs.
A budget controls unnecessary spending such as excessive eating out or impulse shopping and protects important expenses.
slides.note: Budget likho warna wallet khud decide karega!

slides.title: Four Goal Questions
slides.kicker: Chaar sawaal, ek clear money goal.
bullets: The book suggests one simple way to set any financial goal: turn it into four honest questions.
Ask what you want to achieve, how much money you will need, by when you want it, and what steps will help you reach it.
Answering these questions helps people make careful decisions about spending, saving and investing for the future.

items: What do I want to achieve?
How much money will I need?
By when do I want to achieve it?
What steps can help me reach this goal?

slides.note: Goal with a deadline is a plan, not a wish.

slides.title: What Is Saving?
slides.kicker: Thoda aaj bachaya, kal ka suraksha kavach.
bullets: Saving means keeping aside a part of one's income for future use; it is a financial surplus accumulated over time.
Savings are important for comfortable living because life is uncertain and emergencies can arise at any time.
People also save so they can make future investments in assets such as fixed deposits, stocks, mutual funds and real estate.
slides.note: Saving is not leftover money; it is a decision.

slides.title: Why Save At All?
slides.kicker: Life is uncertain; your piggy bank need not be.
bullets: Emergencies do not send an invitation, so savings act as a cushion for uncertain times.
Saving first builds the surplus that investing later needs; no savings means nothing to invest.
The book asks: would you spend ₹100 on a want or a need? Wants and needs, learnt in Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice, guide smart saving.
Even individuals with low income can plan to save; the habit matters as much as the amount.
slides.note: Financial experts suggest saving first, spending what is left.

slides.title: The ₹100 Test
slides.kicker: Sau ka note, badi soch.
bullets: The book asks: if you received ₹100 today, would you save some or all of it, or spend it right away?
From the Grade 9 Part 1 chapter Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice, wants and needs help you decide where money should go.
Choosing needs before wants leaves a surplus, and that surplus is exactly what saving is built on.
slides.note: Chhota amount, badi aadat.

slides.title: Priya vs Sameer
slides.kicker: Same gift, one year later, alag kahani.
bullets: Priya keeps her ₹500 birthday gift in a piggy bank at home; one year later she still has exactly ₹500.
Sameer puts his ₹500 into a savings scheme earning 8 percent interest a year; one year later he has ₹540.
Both are being responsible with money, but they are not doing the same thing: Sameer's money earned a return.
slides.note: Saving and investing are siblings, not twins.

slides.title: Investing Grows Wealth
slides.kicker: Mango tree logic: patience phal deta hai.
bullets: Investing means putting your savings into assets with the aim of protecting their value and generating returns.
It is like planting a mango tree: no fruit immediately, but once it starts, it gives fruit for many years.
Keeping savings in cash provides greater liquidity, but investing increases wealth and protects the value of money.
Investing helps money grow faster than the rate of inflation, so prices rising cannot silently shrink your wealth.
slides.note: Cash sleeps peacefully; invested money works a night shift.

slides.title: Inflation Eats Value
slides.kicker: ₹1,000 bag today, ₹1,060 next year.
bullets: Inflation is the increase in prices of goods and services over time, which reduces the purchasing power of money.
If a school bag costs ₹1,000 today and inflation is 6 percent per year, the same bag may cost about ₹1,060 next year.
Money simply kept at home does not grow, so your purchasing power falls and you may not afford the bag.
Purchasing power is the real-world value of money, measured by what a single unit of currency can buy.
slides.note: Prices chillate rehte hain; money ko bhi chilla-na hai — grow!

slides.title: Magic of Compounding
slides.kicker: Returns par returns — king and sage wala jadoo.
bullets: Compounding is the process where an investment's earnings, such as interest or dividends, are reinvested to generate their own additional earnings over time.
Returns are earned not only on the original investment (the principal) but also on returns already earned, accumulating high returns over time.
The Grade 7 story of the king and the sage from Banks and the Magic of Finance explained this same principle.
Bhavisha saves ₹1,000 a year at 7 percent starting at age 25; Dhruv starts the same at 35, so her money compounds ten years longer.

items: Returns now earn their own returns

slides.note: Start early, let time do the heavy lifting.

slides.title: Four Common Options
slides.kicker: FDs, bonds, stocks, mutual funds — apna menu.
bullets: The book lists four common investment options: fixed deposits, bonds, stocks (equity or shares), and mutual funds.
Each option balances safety, returns and access to money differently, so no single choice fits everyone.
Savings can be deployed across these assets depending on whether a person prefers safety, stable income or growth.
slides.note: Menu dekho, bhookh (goal) ke hisaab se order karo.

slides.title: Fixed Deposits: Safety First
slides.kicker: Neend aa jaati hai FD wale ko.
bullets: Fixed deposits are among the most common and safest investment options, offered by banks and post offices.
A person deposits a lump sum for a fixed period such as one, three or five years at a fixed rate of interest that stays unchanged.
FDs offer assured returns and suit people who prefer safety over high returns.
Government-backed options include the Public Provident Fund (PPF), National Savings Certificate (NSC) and Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana for long-term savings.
slides.note: Safety champions: kam adventure, poori guarantee.

slides.title: Bonds: Lending for Interest
slides.kicker: You become the bank here, dost.
bullets: Bonds are investments through which people lend money to the government or companies, called issuers, for a fixed period.
Buy a ₹10,000 bond paying 5 percent yearly interest and you receive ₹500 after one year; if it matures then, you get ₹10,500 in total.
Maturity periods in reality range from 1 day to 30 years or more, and bonds can often be sold before maturity, making them more liquid.
Government bonds are generally considered safer than corporate bonds and suit those seeking a stable, predictable income.

right.title: Corporate bonds
items: Issuer is a company raising capital

slides.note: Bond = udhaar likhit roop mein, interest ke saath.

slides.title: Stocks: Owning a Piece
slides.kicker: Share kharido, company ke hissedaar bano.
bullets: Shares represent ownership in a company; buying shares makes you a part-owner of that company.
Shareholders may earn returns through dividends as well as an increase in the share price.
The BSE SENSEX is the benchmark index of the Bombay Stock Exchange, tracking 30 large, financially sound, actively traded companies from different sectors.
The SENSEX serves as an important indicator of the overall performance of the Indian stock market.
slides.note: SENSEX = stock market ka report card.

slides.title: Match Option To Need
slides.kicker: Sahi option, sahi maqsad, best combo.
bullets: Prefer safety and assured returns? Fixed deposits at banks or post offices fit best.
Want a stable, predictable income by lending money? Bonds, especially government bonds, are designed for that.
Ready to become a part-owner and accept market ups and downs? Shares offer dividends and possible price gains.
Mutual funds complete the book's list of common options, and schemes like PPF and Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana support long-term saving.
slides.note: There is no best option; there is a best fit.

slides.title: Insurance: A Legal Contract
slides.kicker: Chota premium, badi himmat for emergencies.
bullets: Insurance is a legal contract in which an individual pays a regular amount, called a premium, to an insurance company.
In return, the company agrees to provide financial compensation for specific losses or expenses covered under the policy.
A family may pay ₹500 every month for health insurance; if a member needs treatment, the company covers a large part of the hospital expenses.
Without insurance, the family might have to use a substantial portion of its savings for treatment costs.
slides.note: Premium is rent for your peace of mind.

slides.title: Risk Sharing Pool
slides.kicker: Sab thoda daalte hain, ek ko poori madad.
bullets: Insurance works on the principle of risk sharing: many people pay premiums into a common pool.
In case of any unexpected loss, those insured receive financial support from the insurance company.
Insurance provides security during emergencies, reduces the impact of accidents, illness or property damage, and helps families recover from financial setbacks.
Regular premium payments also encourage people to save and plan their finances.

items: Insured get support from the pool

slides.note: Aam ka achaar jaisa: sab ka contribution, sabki suraksha.

slides.title: Health and Life Insurance
slides.kicker: Sehat bhi, parivaar bhi — dono covered.
bullets: Health insurance covers medical expenses such as hospitalisation, medicines, diagnostic tests and treatments, letting families focus on recovery.
In India, the government scheme Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana provides health coverage to eligible low-income households.
Life insurance supports the family if the policyholder, who may be the breadwinner, passes away.
It helps dependents meet daily expenses, continue children's education and repay loans, ensuring long-term financial security.
slides.note: Health treats the person; life insurance protects the plan.

slides.title: General Insurance
slides.kicker: Gaadi, ghar, fasal, pashu — sab ke liye kavach.
bullets: General insurance protects against losses related to vehicles, homes, businesses and other property.
Motor insurance covers repair costs and damages caused by vehicle accidents.
Property insurance protects homes and businesses against fire, theft, flood, earthquake and other disasters.
Crop insurance covers damages from natural disasters, pests and market price changes, while cattle insurance protects farmers and dairy owners if animals die or are disabled.
slides.note: Farmers ke liye crop and cattle insurance is a lifeline.

slides.title: The Protection Pillar
slides.kicker: Save, invest, insure — poora circle complete.
bullets: Insurance is one of the most effective ways to achieve financial protection, the pillar that safeguards money and assets.
It links back to budgeting and saving: premiums are planned expenses, and compensation protects the savings you worked to build.
Together with investing for growth, insurance ensures that one emergency cannot wipe out years of careful money habits.
slides.note: Growth and protection go hand in hand.

examples.title: Priya and Sameer's ₹500, One Year Later
examples.problem: Priya and Sameer each receive ₹500 as a birthday gift. Priya keeps hers in a piggy bank at home. Sameer puts his into a savings scheme that earns 8 percent interest a year. How much does each have after one year?
steps: Priya's cash at home earns no interest, so it stays ₹500 after one year.
Sameer's yearly interest equals 500 multiplied by 8 divided by 100, which is ₹40.
Add the interest to the original amount: 500 plus 40 equals ₹540.
examples.answer: Priya still has ₹500; Sameer has ₹540, exactly ₹40 more, showing investing generates returns.

examples.title: Bond Interest and Maturity Payout
examples.problem: You buy a bond worth ₹10,000 that pays 5 percent interest per year and matures after one year. How much interest do you earn, and what total amount do you receive at maturity?
steps: Yearly interest equals 10,000 multiplied by 5 divided by 100, which is ₹500.
Bondholders earn this as regular interest, here received after one year.
At maturity the issuer repays the principal too: 10,000 plus 500 equals ₹10,500.
examples.answer: You earn ₹500 interest and receive ₹10,500 in total when the bond matures after one year.

examples.title: Inflation and the School Bag
examples.problem: A school bag costs ₹1,000 today and inflation is 6 percent per year. What will the same bag cost next year, and what does this mean for money kept at home?
steps: Price rise equals 1,000 multiplied by 6 divided by 100, which is ₹60.
Next year's price is about 1,000 plus 60, that is ₹1,060.
Money kept at home does not grow, so your purchasing power falls and you fall ₹60 short for the same bag.
examples.answer: The bag costs about ₹1,060 next year; idle money loses purchasing power, which is why investing aims to grow faster than inflation.

examples.title: A Year of Health Insurance Premiums
examples.problem: A family pays ₹500 every month for health insurance. How much premium do they pay in one full year, and what protection do they get in return?
steps: Yearly premium equals 500 multiplied by 12 months, which is ₹6,000.
Under the policy, the insurance company covers a large part of hospital expenses if a family member needs medical treatment.
Without insurance, the family might have to use a substantial portion of its savings for the same treatment.
examples.answer: The family pays ₹6,000 in a year; in return, covered hospital expenses are largely paid by the company, protecting their savings.

steps.label: Earn income
steps.detail: Salary, business profit, rent, interest or dividends flow in.

steps.label: Budget and set goals
steps.detail: Write a plan that balances income and expenses around clear goals.

steps.label: Save first
steps.detail: Keep aside a surplus for emergencies and future investments.

steps.label: Compare options
steps.detail: Weigh fixed deposits, bonds, stocks and mutual funds.

steps.label: Invest early
steps.detail: Like Bhavisha starting at 25, early money compounds longer.

steps.label: Let it compound
steps.detail: Returns are reinvested and earn their own returns.

steps.label: Insure against risk
steps.detail: Premiums into a common pool protect savings from shocks.

steps.label: Review the plan
steps.detail: Check impulse spending and keep goals on track.
